title: The Ethics of Reading People
hook: Every reading moves information out of someone's body and into your head; ethics is deciding where it is allowed to go next.
why:
The statement at the front of this book sets out the principles: a reading is a guess, attention is not consent, power raises the standard of evidence, and some things this book refuses to teach. Principles are necessary and they are not enough. They tell you what kind of man to be. They do not tell you what to do at half past nine on a Tuesday, when a colleague asks what is going on with someone, and you think you know.

This chapter is the method that sits under the principles. It treats a reading as information that has moved, out of one person's body and into your head, and asks where it may go next. It gives you a test to run before you pass anything on, a short list of what you owe once you have noticed something, a way to find the bias travelling inside your own readings, and a set of hard cases to practise on. The skill of the earlier chapters makes you see more. This one decides whether seeing more makes you better company or worse.

teach.h: A reading is information on the move.
teach.p:
When you notice that a colleague's voice tightens whenever the budget comes up, something has happened that is easy to miss: information has moved. It began in her body, in a meeting, among people who were all there for a shared purpose. Now it is in your head. Nothing wrong has happened yet. All social life runs on movements like this, and she can see your face too. The ethical question is not whether you were allowed to notice. It is where the noticing is allowed to go next.

The philosopher Helen Nissenbaum gave that question a shape. In her account of privacy as contextual integrity, first set out in 2004 and developed in her book *Privacy in Context* in 2010, information is never simply public or private. It arrives under the norms of a context: what a patient tells a doctor, what a colleague shows in a meeting, what a friend lets slip over dinner. Privacy is violated when information flows in ways that break the norms of the context it came from, even if every piece of it was in plain view.

This explains something the public and private split cannot. Your friend's face at his father's funeral was visible to a hundred people. Describing it in a work email the following week would still feel like a betrayal, because a funeral carries norms about what is seen there and where it goes. Nobody had to declare the norms. Everyone present knew them.

Readings deserve more care in transit than facts do, because a reading carries your inference along with what the person showed. When you pass one on, you move not only her tightened voice but your guess about what it meant, and she is not there to correct it. The listener receives a conclusion with the evidence stripped off, and conclusions travel further and faster than the evidence ever would.

Seen this way, the journal is safe for a simple reason. It is a flow from your eyes to your own notebook, kept for your own learning, and that is a context almost everyone would accept.
teach.disconfirm: If the people you read would not mind, when asked plainly, where any of your readings went, the norms of context would not matter for them. Ask one person you trust how they would feel about a particular reading of theirs reaching a particular place, and listen to the answer.
teach.pullQuote: Conclusions travel further and faster than the evidence ever would.

teach.h: Run the flows test before you pass anything on.
teach.p:
Most ethical mistakes in reading people happen in a single sentence, said lightly: *I think she's struggling at home*, *he's clearly not on board*, *she fancies you, by the way*. The test that prevents them takes about ten seconds and has four questions.

First: where did I see this? Name the context and the norms it carried, a team meeting, a dinner among friends, a hospital corridor. Second: what exactly am I passing on, the behaviour or my inference? *She went quiet when the night shift came up* is a report. *She's got problems at home* is a story you built on it. Third: who would receive it, and what could they do with it? A reading that reaches a manager can change someone's work; one that reaches a group can follow her for years. Fourth: would she expect it to go there, and if she learned that it had, would she think it fair?

The fastest way to run the fourth question is backwards. Imagine the person reading the message you are about to send, or standing behind you as you say the sentence. If you would change a word, change it now, or say nothing.

None of this forbids talking about people. Research on reputation, including work by Matthew Feinberg, Robb Willer and their colleagues in 2012, finds that sharing what people have done can protect a group, warning others about someone who cheats or bullies. That is a report of conduct, which the person can answer. A reading of someone's inner state is different. It is a guess about something they have not told anyone, and passing it on takes from them the chance to tell it themselves, or not at all.

When the test fails, there is almost always a better flow available: take what you noticed to the person, or keep it.
teach.disconfirm: If you run the four questions on the last ten readings you passed on and every one passes, either you are already careful or you are answering the fourth question on the other person's behalf. Where you can, ask one of them whether they minded.

teach.p:
Noticing creates a small obligation, and there are three ways to meet it: hold, ask or act. Choosing between them is most of ethics in practice.

Hold is right for most readings. The person showed something, it is theirs, and nothing about the moment needs you. Holding is not ignoring. A reading you keep can still change how you behave, quietly: you slow down, you leave a question for another day, you give the person the easier seat. That is the reading put to its best use, and nobody ever has to know it happened.

Ask is right when the reading touches something you share, such as a plan, a piece of work or a friendship, or when it concerns the person's wellbeing and you are close enough to ask. Ask about the situation, not the signal, and leave a clear way out: *When the night-shift change came up you went quiet. If it causes you a problem, I'd like to know. You don't have to tell me why.* Then accept whatever comes back, including nothing.

Act is for the rare case where there is a risk of harm, to the person or to someone else. Here the norms of context give way to safety, and the guidance at the front of the book on asking directly about suicide is the clearest example. Acting means bringing in help, a crisis line, a doctor, emergency services, the person responsible for safety at work. It never means broadcasting.

The three carry different costs when they are chosen wrongly. Holding when you should have asked costs a little. Asking when you should have held costs a little more, since nobody enjoys being read aloud. Holding when you should have acted can cost a great deal, and it is the error men are most likely to make out of a wish not to intrude.
teach.disconfirm: If over a month you find that your questions about things you noticed regularly leave people feeling watched rather than cared for, you are asking too often or naming their bodies too precisely. Ask less often, and about the situation rather than the signal.
teach.pullQuote: Noticing creates a small debt. Usually it is paid by keeping quiet, or by asking.

teach.p:
Readings do not go wrong at random. They go wrong in the directions a culture has already laid down, and they feel like perception rather than prejudice while they do it.

In 2003 Kurt Hugenberg and Galen Bodenhausen showed White participants short films of faces changing expression, and asked them to mark when anger appeared or faded. Participants higher in implicit prejudice saw anger arrive sooner and linger longer on Black faces than on White ones. Nobody had told them what to see. The bias was inside the act of looking. In 2008 Victoria Brescoll and Eric Uhlmann found that men who expressed anger at work were granted more status, while women who expressed the same anger were granted less, and their anger was put down to their character rather than the situation. The same tight jaw, read through two stereotypes, produced two different people.

A reading kept private is not therefore harmless. It shapes what you do next: how closely you watch someone, how much benefit of the doubt you give, how curtly you answer. A man who reads threat more readily in one group of people will treat that group as more threatening, and will rarely notice that he is doing it.

Introspection will not find this, because the bias feels exactly like seeing. Your ledger can. Tag each scored prediction with the broad group of the person you read, in your own notes only, and after a few months compare the error rates and the direction of the errors. Where you find a gap, such as reading anger or coldness more readily in one group than the record supports, treat your first impression of people in that group as one band less certain until the gap closes.

This is uncomfortable work. It is also the only kind of evidence that can tell you whether your readings are fair.
teach.disconfirm: If your ledger, tagged by group, shows the same error rates and the same direction of errors across groups over a large number of predictions, this bias is not showing up in your readings in that domain. Keep checking, because a small sample from one group can hide a pattern for a long time.

teach.h: The machine that reads faces is a mirror.
teach.p:
Over the past decade companies have sold software that claims to read emotion from faces and voices: in recorded job interviews, in classrooms, in call centres, and in at least one publicly funded trial at European borders. It is worth studying, not because you will build it, but because it is a careless human reader made visible and run at scale.

In 2019 Lisa Feldman Barrett, Ralph Adolphs, Stacy Marsella, Aleix Martinez and Seth Pollak published a long review of the evidence on whether emotions can be read from facial movements. Their conclusion was that people do sometimes scowl when angry and smile when happy, but far less reliably than the products assumed, and that the same face means different things across people, situations and cultures. A scowl can be anger, concentration, confusion or bright sunlight.

The errors also followed the familiar lines. In 2018 Lauren Rhue tested two commercial systems on photographs of professional basketball players and found that they scored Black players as angrier, or more contemptuous, than White players with similar smiles. One large hiring-software company dropped facial analysis from its video interviews in 2021 after sustained criticism. In 2024 the European Union's AI Act banned systems that infer emotions in workplaces and schools, except for medical or safety reasons.

Look at what went wrong and you find this book's warnings, one after another. The systems used a dictionary of expressions. They had no baseline for the person, no knowledge of the context, no way to be shown wrong, and they fed their guesses straight into decisions about people's lives. If that is wrong when a machine does it to millions, it is wrong when you do it to one person. The harm is only smaller.

Whenever you feel sure of a reading, ask whether you would trust a machine that reached it the same way.
teach.disconfirm: If independent tests across cultures and groups showed an automated system inferring specific emotions from faces reliably, without knowing the person or the context, this block would need revising. As of the 2019 review, the evidence pointed the other way.

teach.h: When a reading enters a decision.
teach.p:
The statement at the front of the book says that power raises the standard of evidence. Here is what that means on paper, in the places where a reading can change what happens to someone: hiring, appraisal, discipline, grading, decisions about a child.

Record behaviour, never inference. *He did not make eye contact and gave short answers* can be checked, explained and answered. *He seemed shifty* cannot, and it will be read by people who never met him as a finding. Before you write any impression of demeanour into a record, ask whether it describes the task the person was being judged on. Usually it does not, and it should be left out.

Give the person a chance to answer anything that will count against them. A reading shown to its subject often collapses within a minute: the short answers were a stammer they manage, the lack of eye contact was autism, the flatness was a migraine. A reading that is never shown to its subject never gets that chance, and its errors become permanent.

Prefer structure to impressions. In a large review of personnel research in 1998, Frank Schmidt and John Hunter found that structured interviews, with the same questions asked of everyone and answers scored against a plan, predicted later job performance noticeably better than unstructured conversations. A good part of the difference is that structure leaves less room for the interviewer's reading of the candidate's body to stand in for evidence about the work.

A simple rule covers most cases. If an impression would not survive being read aloud to the person it describes, it should not be in their file. If it would survive, it is probably a description of behaviour, and it can stay.
teach.disconfirm: If decisions in your setting that leave out impressions of demeanour turn out worse, over a fair number of cases, than ones that include them, the rule is too strict for that setting. The research on structured interviews suggests the opposite, but your own records can test it.

teach.p:
At a dinner with an old friend you notice that his wife flinches twice when he gestures sharply near her, and that she checks his face before answering simple questions. You do not know what it means. It could be a startle reflex, an old injury, a row before you arrived, or fear. The flows test rules out the table and the group chat. What you owe is a quiet chance for her to speak: a private moment, a gentle question about how she is, and a way of making sure she knows that help exists, including the domestic abuse lines in your country. You do not confront him on a guess. If you see or hear something that points to immediate danger, you call the emergency services.

A colleague's hands have begun to shake in the mornings, and she has missed two early meetings. The causes run from medication and poor sleep to anxiety, illness and drink, and you are not placed to choose between them. You ask how she is doing, behaviour first, and offer help. If her work is safety-critical, such as driving or operating machinery, the behaviour you saw, not your theory of its cause, can go to whoever is responsible for safety.

Your sixteen-year-old son has come home with the same slumped walk for a week and goes straight to his room. Here you have more access, more duty and more power than in either other case. Use the duty and restrain the power. Sit with him somewhere side by side, say what you have noticed without a verdict, and tell him you are there. The slump is his, and so is the explanation.

In each case the answer came from the same three questions: where the reading came from, what the person would expect, and whether anyone is at risk.
teach.disconfirm: If working through these cases leaves you with a rule that seems to settle every future case automatically, you have learned a rule rather than the method. The test is whether, in a case none of these covers, you can still say where the reading came from and what the person would expect.

poseGallery.doCaption: Taking it, as a question, to the one person it is about.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Passing a reading round the group.
poseGallery.annotation: A reading shared with others reaches people who cannot check it, about someone who cannot answer it. The better flow is almost always to the person, or nowhere.

poseGallery.doCaption: Holding it until there is a private moment and a reason to ask.
poseGallery.annotation: Being right does not settle where a reading may go. Most readings are best held, and a held reading can still make you gentler.

poseGallery.doCaption: Listening, and recording only what was said and done.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Writing the impression into the file.
poseGallery.annotation: A record of behaviour can be checked and answered. A record of demeanour is read later as a finding by people who never met the person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking whether you would read it the same way on a different face.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sure that the anger on that face is obvious.
poseGallery.annotation: Bias feels exactly like perception. Only a ledger tagged by group can show whether your first impressions are fair.

poseGallery.doCaption: Putting the phone down and asking later, in private
poseGallery.dontCaption: Typing a reading into the group chat
poseGallery.annotation: Most ethical mistakes happen in a single light sentence. A minute's pause is enough to run the flows test.

poseGallery.doCaption: Going to him, side by side, with one question
poseGallery.dontCaption: Saying nothing to a friend for months
poseGallery.annotation: Holding everything out of fear of intruding can leave someone who needed to be noticed with nobody.

caseStudy:
Tom, forty-four, manages a team of maintenance engineers at a distribution centre. At a Monday briefing his director announces that the night shift will be reorganised and that everyone will take a turn. Tom notices that Priya, one of his best engineers, goes very still and pale, writes nothing down, and leaves before the usual coffee. Over the next week she stops eating lunch with the team.

On Thursday evening, at the pub, his colleague Gary asks what is up with Priya. Tom feels the pull of a ready answer. He thinks something is going on at home, and he has the beginnings of a theory. He runs the flows test instead. He saw her stillness in a work briefing; the theory about home is his, not hers; Gary has no role in her work; and if Priya heard that her private life was being discussed in the pub, she would be right to be angry. He says he has no idea and would rather not guess.

The next morning he finds her alone in the workshop and asks about the situation, not the signal. *When the night-shift change came up you went quiet. If it causes you a problem, I'd like to know. You don't have to tell me why.* She is silent for a moment, then tells him that she cares for her mother in the evenings and that nights are impossible. They work out a swap with two engineers who want the night premium.

A month later the director asks Tom to note "attitude concerns" in Priya's appraisal, because she looked unenthusiastic about the reorganisation. Tom writes what she did: raised a scheduling conflict promptly and helped arrange cover. He leaves out the impression, and tells the director why: it would not survive being read aloud to her, and it was wrong.

Gary never finds out about Priya's mother. Nobody needed him to.
observe: Notice one moment this week when you are tempted to tell a third person what you read in someone, and ask yourself whether that person would expect it to travel there.
In a meeting or a group chat, notice when someone's reading of another person, such as he's not on board, is passed round as fact, and work out what behaviour, if any, it was built from.

Find one advert, article or product that claims to read emotions from faces or voices, and note which of the following it ignores: the person's baseline, the context, and any way of being shown wrong.

drills.name: Flows Audit
steps: Open the last two weeks of your journal and list every reading you passed on to anyone, in speech or in writing.
For each, write the context you first saw it in and the norms that context carried.
Mark whether you passed on the behaviour or your inference about it.
Mark any flow the person would not have expected or would not have thought fair.
For each marked flow, write what you would do differently, and whether you now owe the person anything.
variations: Do the audit for readings you passed on outside work too, such as to family or friends, and compare.
Mark which of the flows you would be comfortable describing to the person concerned, word for word.
Notice the next reading you are tempted to pass on, and write down the flows test answers before deciding.

drills.name: Behaviour, Not Verdict
steps: Write down five impressions you have formed or voiced about people at work or at home, such as seemed shifty or not committed.
Rewrite each one as observable behaviour with a time and place, removing every word that describes character.
Read the two versions side by side and note how much of the original was inference.
Mark which rewritten versions would survive being read aloud to the person.
Keep only those, and decide whether any of them is worth saying at all.
variations: Ask a trusted colleague to rewrite one of your impressions as behaviour without seeing your version, and compare.
Read back the last reference or appraisal you wrote and check every adjective for the behaviour behind it.
Practise saying one rewritten version aloud as you would to the person, and notice whether it feels fair.

drills.name: Bias Audit
steps: Take your scored predictions from the calibration ledger, at least forty of them.
Tag each with the broad group of the person you read, in your own notes only.
For each group, work out the hit rate and note the direction of the misses, for example readings of anger or coldness that did not come true.
Write down any group where your misses lean one way more than for others.
Write one adjustment, such as treating first impressions of that group as one band less certain, and set a date to check it again.
variations: Tag your predictions by the person's age and seniority as well as by group, and look for any lean in your misses.
Ask a friend from a different background to look at your tags and tell you what they notice.
Repeat the audit after three months and see whether the adjustment you wrote has changed the pattern.

drills.name: Hold, Ask or Act
steps: Write down three things you have noticed about people in the past fortnight that you have not yet done anything about.
For each, decide whether it calls for holding, asking or acting, and write one sentence saying why.
For any you marked act, write the specific risk of harm that justifies it, and who you would bring in.
For any you marked ask, write the exact question, about the situation rather than the signal, with a clear way out.
Say the question aloud twice, as you would say it to the person.
variations: For each reading you marked hold, write what you will quietly do differently because of it.
For each reading you marked act, write the proper route for acting in your setting, such as who you would tell.
Discuss one of your hold-ask-act choices with a trusted friend, without names, and see whether they would choose the same.

drills.name: Hard Case Rehearsal
steps: Choose one hard case from this chapter, or one of your own with the names and details changed.
Write where the reading came from and the norms of that context.
List every person who might receive the reading and what they could do with it.
Write what you owe, the first sentence you would say, and to whom.
Write one piece of information that would change your plan, and what you would do instead.
variations: Rehearse one hard case aloud with a friend playing the person you are worried about, using your first sentence.
Find out the proper reporting route at your workplace for safeguarding or welfare concerns, so that you know it before you need it.
Write a hard case of your own from a past situation you now think you handled badly, and plan how you would handle it now.

quiz.q: You have read, correctly as it turns out, that a colleague is anxious about her job. What does being right allow you to do?
options: Mention it to others who work with her, since it is true and they may be able to help
Record it in your notes on her, since accurate readings are evidence worth keeping
Being right does not settle where it may go; that depends on where you saw it and what she would expect
Tell her you knew all along, so that she does not have to explain herself to you
quiz.explain: Accuracy and appropriateness are different questions. A true reading passed to the wrong place is still a breach of the norms it came from, and it takes from her the choice of whether and how to tell her own story.

quiz.q: In Helen Nissenbaum's account of privacy as contextual integrity, when is privacy violated?
options: When information flows in ways that break the norms of the context it came from
Whenever personal information about someone is observed by anyone without permission
Only when information about a person is written down or recorded in some way
Only when the information was secret and someone deliberately revealed it
quiz.explain: Contextual integrity explains why information seen in plain view can still be misused. What matters is whether its next move fits the norms under which it was shown, such as a meeting, a funeral or a dinner among friends.

quiz.q: At dinner your friend's wife flinches twice when he gestures sharply near her and checks his face before answering. What fits this chapter?
options: Raise it quietly with the others at the table, to see whether they noticed the same thing
Confront your friend later about how he treats her, and tell him what you saw at dinner
Do nothing, since you cannot know what it means and it is not your business to ask
Find a private moment to ask her gently how she is, and make sure she knows help exists
quiz.explain: You cannot know what the flinch means, which rules out accusation and broadcasting. You can give her a safe chance to speak and make sure she knows where help is. If anything points to immediate danger, call the emergency services.

quiz.q: What did the 2019 review led by Lisa Feldman Barrett conclude about reading emotions from faces?
options: Faces reveal emotions as reliably as words do, once you know which muscles to watch
Facial movements vary too much across people, settings and cultures to be read as emotions without context
Only trained professionals can read emotions from faces with any real reliability
Machines can now read emotions from faces better than people are able to
quiz.explain: The review found some link between expressions and emotions but far less reliable than commercial systems assumed. A scowl can be anger, concentration, confusion or sun in the eyes, which is why baseline and context matter.

quiz.q: Which statement about readings you keep to yourself is most accurate?
options: They are harmless, because nobody else ever hears them and so nobody is affected
They are fine as long as they turn out to be accurate when you check them later
They still shape how you treat people, so a biased private reading does harm even when it is never spoken
They should always be shared with the person, so that they can be checked and corrected
quiz.explain: A reading you keep changes how closely you watch someone, how much benefit of the doubt you give and how you answer them. That is why bias in private readings matters, and why the ledger, not introspection, is the place to look for it.

quiz.q: Your director asks you to note attitude concerns in a staff member's appraisal because she looked unenthusiastic in a meeting. What fits?
options: Write it as asked, since the director saw the meeting too and is entitled to a view
Write that she seemed unenthusiastic in the meeting, but add a note saying that you disagree with it
Ask the other staff who were there whether they noticed the same lack of enthusiasm
Record what she did and said, leave out the impression, and raise any concern with her directly
quiz.explain: Impressions of demeanour in a record are later read as findings by people who never met her, and she cannot answer them. Behaviour can be checked and answered. If there is a concern, the person it is about should hear it first.

quiz.q: What did Hugenberg and Bodenhausen find in their 2003 study of faces changing expression?
options: That everyone saw anger appear and fade at exactly the same moments on every face
That people higher in implicit prejudice saw anger arrive sooner and linger longer on Black faces
That participants could not detect anger at all on any of the faces that were shown to them in short films
That anger was always seen more clearly on White faces than on Black faces by every participant
quiz.explain: Participants higher in implicit prejudice saw anger arrive sooner and linger longer on Black faces than on White ones. The bias was inside the act of looking, before any conscious judgment.

quiz.q: In a work group chat, a colleague speculates that another colleague's marriage is in trouble because he looked upset in a meeting. What fits this chapter best?
options: Add what you saw in the car park, since it helps everyone understand what is happening
Add nothing to the thread, redirect it lightly, and ask him privately whether he is all right
Report the colleague who posted to HR at once, since any speculation is a serious offence
Ignore it completely and mute the thread, since nothing about the speculation has anything to do with you
quiz.explain: The flows test rules out the chat: the reading came from a work meeting, the story about his marriage is inference and rumour, and he would not expect it to go there. A private question about the situation is the right flow.

quiz.q: Someone says software that reads emotions from faces is free of human bias. What did Lauren Rhue find when she tested two commercial systems?
options: That they scored Black basketball players as angrier or more contemptuous than White players with similar smiles
That they read every face identically, whatever the person's background, age or expression
That they were far more accurate than trained human observers at detecting genuine emotions in every face shown
That they could not process photographs of basketball players at all, and simply returned no results whatsoever
quiz.explain: Rhue found racial differences in how two commercial systems scored similar smiles. Software built on human-labelled data can carry, and scale up, the biases of human readers.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time when something you noticed about a person travelled further than it should have: told to a colleague, written in a message, or used in a decision. Where did you first see it, and what would the person have expected to happen to it? Who did it reach, and could they correct it? If it happened again tomorrow, what would you do differently at the moment of telling, and do you still owe that person anything?
reflection.guidance: You are looking for one flow, not a general confession. Most people find their example in a light remark that seemed harmless at the time. Name the context it came from and the exact sentence you said, if you can remember it. If you decide you owe the person something, it is usually small: a correction to whoever heard the reading, or simply never repeating it.

failureMode: There are two opposite failures. The first is to run the flows test after the fact, as a way of feeling better about something already said, so that the test becomes a ritual of absolution rather than a check. The second is paralysis: a man becomes so worried about intruding that he holds everything, including the reading that needed a question or the one that needed help. The cost of that failure is quieter but can be far greater, because the person who needed someone to notice gets nobody. There is a third, subtler failure. Having a careful method can make a reader feel entitled to read more, more closely, more often. The point of this chapter is the opposite: to read with lighter hands, ask sooner, and carry less.

moreCases.title: The team leader who guessed a pregnancy
moreCases.scene:
Aidan, thirty-six, leads a small product team at a software company, and he is good at noticing things. Over two weeks, he notices that one of his developers, Emma, thirty-one, has stopped drinking coffee, has left two meetings suddenly looking pale, has turned down a drink at the Friday social and has started wearing looser clothes. He puts the signs together and is fairly sure she is pregnant.

At the Friday social, while Emma is at the bar, a colleague asks Aidan why Emma has been so off lately. Aidan, pleased with his reading and wanting to defend her, says quietly, "I think she might be expecting. Keep it to yourself." He means it kindly.

By Monday, half the team knows. Someone congratulates Emma in the kitchen. Emma goes white, says nothing and goes back to her desk.

On Tuesday, Emma asks to speak to Aidan. She tells him that she is twelve weeks pregnant, that she had a miscarriage last year, and that she had decided not to tell anyone at work until her scan on Friday, in case it happened again. She had not even told her mother. She asks him how the whole team came to know before her own family did.

He had also noticed, he realises afterwards, that Emma had been careful not to mention anything herself, and had taken that as shyness rather than as a decision.
moreCases.misread:
Aidan read the signs correctly, and read passing them on as a kindness, a way of explaining Emma's behaviour sympathetically. Emma read the congratulations in the kitchen as a disclosure taken from her before she was ready to make it.

The colleague who asked had read the reply as confidential, and told only two people, each of whom told two more, which is how a reading travels.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter's central idea, drawing on Helen Nissenbaum's account of privacy as contextual integrity, is that a reading is information on the move, and that ethics is deciding where it is allowed to go. Aidan's reading began in Emma's body, at work, among colleagues, and moved, through one light sentence, into a context she had not chosen and would not have expected. Being right did not make the flow acceptable; it made it more harmful. The flows test would have stopped him: where did I see this, am I passing on behaviour or inference, who will receive it, and would she expect it to go there? The answer was to hold. Aidan apologised to Emma without excuses, asked whether there was anything she wanted him to say to the team, and followed her wishes exactly. He also told the colleague, privately, that he had been wrong to speculate. Emma's scan on Friday was fine.

Emma told the team herself, a week later, in her own words, and asked Aidan to sit beside her when she did.

moreCases.title: The teacher who noticed the bruises
moreCases.scene:
Ms Rahman, forty-one, teaches a Year 4 class. One of her pupils, a quiet eight-year-old boy, has been arriving at school tired and hungry for a few weeks. In PE on Wednesday, as he changes, she notices bruises on his upper arms, in a pattern that looks to her like the marks of fingers. When a classmate bumps into him, he flinches more than seems normal. When she asks him, gently, whether he is all right, he says he fell over.

Ms Rahman feels the pull of several responses. She wants to ask him more questions, to find out what happened. She thinks about ringing his mother that evening. She mentions it, quietly, to a teaching assistant in the corridor, who says that the family has had a hard time recently and that the mother seems lovely. Ms Rahman starts to wonder whether she is overreacting.

She remembers the school's safeguarding training, and the section of this chapter on what you owe after noticing.

At the end of the day, she goes to the school's designated safeguarding lead, Mr Foster, and tells him exactly what she saw, when and what the boy said, in his words.

The boy's file mentions that his father recently left the family home. The teaching assistant's remark had been well meant, and it had nearly talked Ms Rahman out of acting.
moreCases.misread:
Ms Rahman's first instincts were to investigate herself, to contact the family or to talk it over informally, and the teaching assistant's reassurance nearly led her to read her own concern as an overreaction.

The teaching assistant read her own reassurance as kindness to a struggling family, without considering what it might mean for the child, who has no voice in that conversation and depends on adults to notice and pass concerns on.
moreCases.betterRead: This chapter describes three responses to noticing: hold, ask or act, and says that acting is right when there is a risk of harm that makes it wrong to wait. A possible injury to a child is exactly that case, and in schools the way to act is set out in safeguarding procedures: tell the designated safeguarding lead promptly, record what you saw and what the child said in their own words, and do not investigate, question the child at length or contact the family yourself, which could put the child at risk or compromise any later enquiry. The teaching assistant's comment, passed in a corridor, was the wrong flow, and Ms Rahman's decision not to repeat it was right. Mr Foster took her written account and followed the school's procedures, contacting the local authority's children's services. Ms Rahman did not learn the outcome, which is often the case, and was told that she had done exactly the right thing by passing on what she saw rather than what she guessed.

moreCases.title: The patient labelled drug-seeking
moreCases.scene:
Beth, thirty, is a nurse on an acute medical ward. At handover one morning, the night nurse describes a patient, Mr Adeyemi, twenty-eight, as "drug-seeking". He has been restless all night, pressing the call bell, asking repeatedly for more pain relief, and he became angry when told he would have to wait. The night nurse's written note says: "Demanding, aggressive manner, drug-seeking behaviour."

Beth goes to see him. He is lying curled on his side, sweating, holding his abdomen, and he tells her through gritted teeth that he has sickle cell disease and that this is a crisis, the worst he has had in a year. He says that every time he comes into hospital, someone decides he is after drugs.

Beth checks his notes. His diagnosis is recorded on the front page. His pain scores overnight were nine and ten out of ten. The note about drug-seeking has already been read by the doctor on the morning ward round, who has reduced his pain relief.

Beth thinks about the note. She also thinks about the chapter's section on what happens when a reading enters a decision.

The night nurse, Beth learns later, had had a difficult shift, with two other patients deteriorating, and had written the note at the end of twelve hours on her feet.
moreCases.misread:
The night nurse read Mr Adeyemi's restlessness, repeated requests and anger as drug-seeking, and wrote that inference into his notes. The doctor read the note as a clinical finding and acted on it, reducing the treatment for a patient in severe pain.

Mr Adeyemi, for his part, read the reduced pain relief as one more confirmation that he would never be believed in hospital, which made him more distressed and, to the staff, more demanding.
moreCases.betterRead: This chapter says that when a reading enters a decision, power raises the standard of evidence: record behaviour, never inference. "Pressed the call bell eleven times; asked for more analgesia; pain score nine" can be checked and explained. "Drug-seeking behaviour" cannot, and it travelled straight into a decision about his treatment. The section on bias adds that readings go wrong in the directions a culture has laid down, and that labels like this one are not applied evenly. Beth's better response was to act, because the patient was at risk of harm. She told the doctor at once what she had seen, gave the pain scores and the diagnosis, and asked for the pain relief to be reviewed, which it was. She then spoke to the nurse in charge about the note. It was amended to describe behaviour, and the ward added a reminder to its handover guidance about labels.

moreCases.title: The friend who said nothing
moreCases.scene:
Jake, forty, has known his friend Craig since school. Over the past six months, Craig has changed. He has been drinking more, sometimes texting at two in the morning. He has missed the last three five-a-side games. When they meet, he looks tired and thinner, and he changes the subject whenever Jake asks about his job. Jake has noticed all of it.

He has also read this chapter, and taken its warnings seriously. He does not want to intrude. He does not want to make assumptions about Craig's private life, or diagnose him, or pass on a reading. So he holds. He says nothing to Craig, and nothing to anyone else. He tells himself that Craig will talk when he is ready, and that it is not his place.

In the spring, Craig's sister rings Jake. Craig has been signed off work with depression, and is staying with her for a while. She says that he had been struggling for months, that he had lost his job in the autumn and had told nobody, and that he had said, the night before, that he wished one of his friends had asked.

Jake sits in his car outside the house for a long time after the call.

He had once nearly asked, in the car after a game Craig did come to, and had stopped himself because it seemed like prying.
moreCases.misread:
Jake read the chapter's warnings about intrusion as a reason to hold everything, and read his own silence as respect. Craig read his friends' silence as a sign that nobody had noticed, or that nobody wanted to know.

Craig's other friends had read the missed games the same way, as Craig being busy, and had each assumed that someone else would ask.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter's failure mode names exactly this: paralysis, when a man becomes so worried about intruding that he holds everything, including the reading that needed a question or the one that needed help. The cost is quieter but can be far greater, because the person who needed someone to notice gets nobody. The chapter distinguishes holding, asking and acting. Craig's changes, sustained over months, called for asking: a private moment, a question about the situation rather than a verdict, and a way out if he did not want to talk. Something like "You've seemed knackered for a while, and I've missed you at football. How are things, really?" would have cost Jake nothing. His better response, late as it was, was to visit Craig at his sister's, sit with him, and say that he was sorry he had not asked. He then kept turning up, every week, side by side, as the chapter on masculinity in Part V describes.

Craig told him, months later, that the weekly visits had mattered more than anything anyone said.

workedReading.title: A reading in the group chat
workedReading.scene:
Ewan, thirty-three, is one of eight people in a work group chat, set up for a project team but now used mostly for jokes and gossip. On a Thursday evening, a colleague, Rhona, posts: "Did anyone else notice Dev in the client meeting today? He looked like he was about to cry. Think his marriage is in trouble, he's had a face on all week." Two people react with a crying emoji. Another replies, "Yeah, I heard his wife moved out." Ewan was in the meeting. He noticed Dev too: quiet, red-eyed, looking at the table. He also feels a strong pull to add what he knows, which is that Dev took a long personal call in the car park at lunchtime. He has the reply half typed when he stops and runs the flows test from this chapter.

He also knows that Rhona is not unkind. She is worried about Dev, in her way. Most readings that go wrong in group chats start with someone who cares, which is part of why they spread so easily.

steps.label: Pause before replying
steps.text:
He deletes the half-typed message and puts the phone down for a minute. Most ethical mistakes in reading people happen in a single sentence, said lightly, as this chapter warns, and a group chat is designed for exactly that kind of sentence: quick, casual, and instantly passed to everyone at once. A minute's pause is enough to ask the four questions.

He also notices how much he wants to post his piece of information, and recognises the small pleasure of being the one who knows. It is a feeling worth noticing, and not trusting.

steps.label: Where did I see this?
steps.text:
He saw Dev in a client meeting and in the car park, at work, among colleagues. The norms of that context allow colleagues to notice that someone seems upset, and perhaps to ask whether they are all right. They do not include speculating about his marriage to a group of eight people, most of whom were not there.

He also reminds himself that the chat has eight members, one of whom reports directly to Dev's manager, and that anything posted there could reach places Dev would never expect.

steps.label: Behaviour or inference?
steps.text:
What he actually saw was behaviour: red eyes, quietness, a long phone call. "His marriage is in trouble" is Rhona's inference, and "his wife moved out" is a rumour from someone else entirely. The chat has already turned a few observations into a story about Dev's private life, and his own message would have added another piece of evidence to it.

He also notes that red eyes in a meeting could mean a dozen things, including hay fever, tiredness or news about someone else entirely.

steps.label: Would Dev expect this flow?
steps.text:
He asks himself whether Dev would expect his red eyes in a client meeting to become a thread about his marriage in a chat he is not part of, and whether Dev would think the flow reasonable if he saw it. The answer to both is no. That settles it: whatever he does, he will not add to the thread.

He also imagines Dev reading the thread over someone's shoulder, which makes the answer even clearer.

steps.label: Choose: hold, ask or act
steps.text:
He decides that the reading calls for asking, not for passing on. Dev seemed genuinely upset, and Ewan works alongside him. There is no sign of immediate risk that would call for acting. He will find a private moment tomorrow, ask a question about the situation rather than offering a verdict, and give Dev an easy way to say he is fine.

He also decides that, if Dev says he is fine, he will believe him and leave it there, rather than pressing for a reason.

steps.label: Redirect the chat
steps.text:
He picks up the phone and writes, lightly: "Probably best to leave Dev's stuff to Dev. I'll check he's OK tomorrow." He adds nothing else. Nobody replies for a few minutes. Then Rhona writes "Fair enough", and someone posts about the football. The thread about Dev stops. Ewan notices that a short sentence was enough to change the flow, which is what this chapter's drills rehearse.

He also does not lecture the group, which would have turned a redirection into a confrontation and made people defensive.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The next morning, Ewan catches Dev at the coffee machine and says, "You seemed a bit rough yesterday. Everything all right? No need to say if not." Dev says that his father has been taken into hospital and that it does not look good. He has told nobody at work. Ewan asks whether there is anything he can cover, and takes the client follow-up off Dev's list. Later, Ewan quietly asks the chat's creator whether the group could be closed now that the project is over.

He also does not tell the chat what Dev told him, which, he realises, would have been the same mistake in a kinder form.

moreFailures.title: Reading people for entertainment
moreFailures.body:
Once you have learned to read bodies, it is tempting to use the skill as a game: commenting on strangers in a café, guessing aloud about a couple's relationship at the next table, analysing a date's nervousness to friends afterwards, or narrating what a colleague's posture says about them at lunch. It can feel harmless and even clever. But each comment moves information out of someone's body and into a context they never chose, which is exactly what this chapter asks you to check before doing. The people being read cannot answer, correct or object, and the readings are usually wrong in the ways the bias section describes. The skills in this book are for understanding people you deal with and helping where you can. If you notice that you are mostly using them to entertain others at someone else's expense, put them down.

A useful test is whether you would be comfortable if the stranger you were analysing overheard every word.

moreFailures.title: Treating body-language readings of public figures as fact
moreFailures.body:
Politicians, celebrities and people accused of crimes are often the subject of confident body-language analysis: commentators claim that a touch of the nose shows a lie, that a smile proves guilt, that a pause reveals a secret. These readings spread widely, and the people concerned usually cannot answer them. The evidence does not support them. Part I's chapter on deception showed how weak the link is between behaviour and lying, and Barrett and colleagues' 2019 review concluded that emotions cannot be reliably inferred from facial movements alone. Public figures have less privacy in many respects, but the reading is no more accurate for being about someone famous. If you share or repeat such analysis, you are passing on an inference as if it were a fact, and often one shaped by the reader's existing opinion of the person.

If you are going to comment on a public figure, describe what they did and leave out what you think it means.

moreFailures.title: Telling people what they feel
moreFailures.body:
"You're angry." "You're nervous." "You're obviously upset about this." Telling someone what they are feeling, especially in front of others, turns a private state into a public verdict and puts the person in the position of either confirming it or arguing with you about their own inner life. The chapter's pose gallery shows the alternative: hold the reading until there is a private moment and a reason to ask, and then ask about the situation rather than announcing the feeling. "You went quiet when the deadline came up. Is the timing a problem?" respects the person's authority over their own experience; "You're stressed about the deadline" claims it. You may be right about the feeling. Even so, it is theirs to name, and naming it for them often makes them less, not more, willing to talk.

If you genuinely need to name a feeling, offer it as a question: "Am I right that this is frustrating?"

moreFailures.title: Trusting the machine over the person
moreFailures.body:
Software that claims to read emotion from faces and voices is increasingly used in hiring, education and security, and it can seem more objective than a human reader. This chapter describes it as a careless human reader made visible and run at scale. Barrett and colleagues' review found that the same facial movement can express different emotions in different people and contexts, and Rhue found that commercial systems scored Black basketball players as angrier or more contemptuous than White players with similar smiles. If you work somewhere that uses such tools, do not treat their outputs as evidence about a person's feelings, honesty or suitability. Ask what the tool claims, what evidence supports it, whether it has been tested for bias and whether people are told it is being used. And where a person and a machine disagree about how someone feels, believe the person.

If you are asked to use such a tool, it is reasonable to ask for the evidence behind it before you agree.

questions.q: Is it wrong to notice things about people?
questions.a:
No. Noticing is part of all social life, and the people around you can see your face too, as this chapter says. The ethical question is not whether you were allowed to notice but where the information goes next. A reading that stays in your head and quietly changes how you behave, by slowing down, leaving a question for another day or giving someone the easier seat, is often exactly right. Problems arise when readings move: into a conversation with a third person, a group chat, a written note, a decision about someone's job or care. That is where the flows test matters: where did I see this, am I passing on behaviour or inference, who will receive it, and would the person expect it to go there?

It also helps to notice how often you pass on readings without meaning to, through a raised eyebrow or a knowing look to someone else.

questions.q: When should I act rather than ask?
questions.a:
When there is a risk of harm that makes waiting wrong. This chapter's examples include a possible injury to a child, as Ms Rahman saw; a patient whose treatment is being affected by a wrong label, as Beth found; and someone who may be in danger. In those cases, acting usually means following the proper route rather than investigating yourself: telling a safeguarding lead, a senior colleague, a doctor or, in an emergency, the emergency services. Record what you saw and heard, not what you guessed. Do not confront the person you are worried about, or anyone you suspect, in a way that could make things worse for the person at risk. Outside those situations, asking, privately and gently, is usually the better choice.

If you are unsure whether a situation calls for acting, ask the person whose job it is, such as a safeguarding lead or a senior nurse, for advice. That is itself a proper flow.

questions.q: What should I say if someone asks me what I think is going on with another person?
questions.a: Run the flows test before you answer. Often the most honest reply is to say what you saw, in behavioural terms, and to decline to add your inference: "She did seem quiet in the meeting. I don't know why." If the question is gossip, as it was in Ewan's group chat, a light redirection works well: "Probably best to leave that to her," or "I'll check she's OK." If the person asking has a legitimate role, such as a manager concerned about someone's welfare, you can suggest they ask the person directly rather than relying on your reading. Avoid confirming theories about someone's private life, health or relationships, however sympathetic the intention. Aidan's kindly meant answer at the Friday social is the case to remember.

questions.q: Should I tell someone I have noticed that they seem upset?
questions.a:
Often yes, if you do it privately, gently and with an easy way out. Ask about the situation rather than announcing the feeling: "You seemed a bit rough yesterday. Everything all right? No need to say if not," as Ewan did at the coffee machine. Choose a private moment, not a meeting or a group. Accept whatever answer you get, including "I'm fine", and do not press. The chapter's failure mode warns that holding everything out of fear of intruding can leave someone who needed to be noticed with nobody, as Craig was. A kind, private question costs very little, and it tells the person that someone saw them and cares, which is often what matters most.

If they do want to talk, listen more than you speak, and ask what would help rather than offering solutions straight away.

questions.q: Is it ethical to analyse politicians' body language?
questions.a: You can notice what public figures do, as anyone can, but be very careful about what you conclude and what you pass on. The evidence does not support reading lies, guilt or hidden motives from body language, as Part I's chapter on deception and Barrett and colleagues' review both make clear. Your readings are also likely to be shaped by what you already think of the person. If you discuss a politician's performance, describe behaviour, such as "he paused for a long time before answering", rather than claiming to know what it meant. Be wary of commentators who claim certainty, and avoid sharing confident analyses of people accused of crimes, whose trials and reputations can be affected by public readings that have no basis.

questions.q: How can I tell whether my readings are biased?
questions.a:
Mostly by looking at your own record, because bias feels like perception rather than prejudice while it is happening. The Bias Audit drill uses your calibration ledger: tag your scored predictions by the broad group of the person you read, and see whether your misses lean in a particular direction for some groups. Hugenberg and Bodenhausen found that people higher in implicit prejudice saw anger arrive sooner and linger longer on Black faces, and Brescoll and Uhlmann found that the same expression of anger was read differently in men and women. Use the swap test from Part IV and Part V: would you read the same behaviour the same way in someone different? And where a reading enters a decision, write behaviour, not inference, so that others can check it.

It also helps to invite colleagues to point out when your readings seem to lean one way, and to thank them when they do.

watch.title: You aren't at the mercy of your emotions
watch.notice: Lisa Feldman Barrett argues that emotions are constructed by the brain and that faces do not carry fixed meanings. Notice how her argument supports the chapter's caution against confident readings of other people.

reviewPrompt: Before passing on any reading this week, name where you first saw it and decide whether the person would expect it to travel to the place you are sending it.
